summary.text: In Big Bang models, the age of the universe is the cosmological time back to the point where the scale factor of the universe extrapolates to zero.
Using the latest models and data from the Planck project, the age of the universe is 13.8 billion years.
Astronomers use two approaches, one matched to features of the early universe and one based on a ladder of stars, and they give slightly different Hubble constants.

items.prompt: A physicist in the 1800s reasons that a closed system that has existed forever would settle at one temperature. What follows for an infinitely old universe?

options.label: It would be hotter at its centre than at its edges
It would be growing steadily larger in every direction
It would hold no stars and no life, so its age is likely finite
It would hold more stars than any telescope could count

items.explain: Entropy dictates that an infinitely old universe would be at one temperature everywhere, so there would be no stars and no life; this hinted the age may be finite.

items.prompt: Why do the two ways of working out the universe's age lean on different parts of cosmic history?

options.label: One uses features from very early times, the other local measurements from late times
One uses only the oldest stars, the other only planets
One counts galaxies, the other counts years on Earth
One was made before Einstein, the other after Hubble

items.explain: The Lambda-CDM method is matched to features from very early in the universe, while the star ladder depends on local measurements late in its history.

items.prompt: Spectra from distant galaxies show lines shifted toward red, and the dimmer a galaxy looks, the bigger the shift. What did astronomers take from this?

options.label: The farther a galaxy is, the brighter its stars must be
The farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away, so the universe is expanding
Distant galaxies are slowing down as they approach us
The universe is steady and every galaxy sits still

items.explain: Greater redshift for more distant galaxies meant they seemed to move away faster, the first direct evidence that the universe is not static but expanding.

items.prompt: Hubble's first estimate of the universe's age came out very low. Why?

options.label: He assumed the galaxies were moving much faster than they are
He used a stellar age that was too old
He ignored the redshift of the galaxies altogether
He assumed the galaxies were much closer than they are

items.explain: The first estimate came from when all objects must have started speeding out from one point, and Hubble assumed galaxies were much closer than later found.

items.prompt: An antenna picks up a steady microwave hum from all of the sky, day and night, and it is not from Earth, the Sun or the Milky Way. What did two teams conclude?

options.label: It is just noise made by the antenna's own electronic circuits
It is radiation left over from the Big Bang, strong evidence for that theory
It is light coming from the very oldest star in the galaxy
It is heat given off by the far side of the Sun at night

items.explain: Penzias and Wilson's signal and the search by Dicke, Peebles and Wilkinson came together: the noise was radiation left over from the Big Bang.

items.prompt: The Methuselah star is estimated at 14.27 ± 0.80 billion years while the universe is 13.8. Is that a contradiction?

options.label: Yes, a star can never be older than its estimate
Yes, the universe must be revised to be older
No, the star's margin of error makes the two values compatible
No, the star was formed before the universe began

items.explain: Both values are compatible with the Planck 2018 number once the uncertainty is included.

paragraphs.heading: Running the clock backward
paragraphs.text: Because the universe is expanding, the equation that describes its expansion can be run backward to where it began. In Big Bang models, the universe's age is the cosmological time since that point, where the scale factor reaches zero. The latest models, using data from the Planck project, put that age at 13.8 billion years.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to measure it
paragraphs.text: Astronomers have two routes to the answer. One uses Lambda-CDM, a model of the early universe built on particle physics, and matches it to features from very early on, such as the cosmic microwave background. The other uses the distances and relative speeds of a ladder made of several kinds of stars, so it relies on nearby measurements from late in cosmic history. The two give slightly different values for the Hubble constant, which goes into a formula for the age. The range of the estimate also overlaps the estimated age of the oldest star observed.

paragraphs.heading: An eternal universe
paragraphs.text: In the 18th century, the idea that Earth was millions or even billions of years old started to appear. Still, most scientists through the 19th century and into the early 20th assumed the universe itself was eternal and in a steady state, with no change at the largest scales then known. The first scientific hint that its age might be finite came from thermodynamics, set out in the mid-19th century. Entropy implies that an infinitely old universe would have everything at one temperature, leaving no stars and no life.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein and Hubble
paragraphs.text: In 1915 Albert Einstein published general relativity, and in 1917 he built the first cosmological model on it. To fit a steady-state universe, he added a term later called the cosmological constant, but Arthur Eddington showed his static model was unstable. The first direct hint of expansion came in a 1929 work that combined recession speeds of galaxies, measured mostly by Vesto Slipher, with Edwin Hubble's distances to them. The light of these galaxies was shifted toward the red, suggesting they were moving away from Earth, and the farther away a galaxy seemed, the faster it seemed to recede.

paragraphs.heading: First estimates
paragraphs.text: The first age estimate came from working out when all those galaxies must have started rushing away from one point. Hubble's first figure was very low, since the galaxies were thought to be far nearer than they later turned out to be. In 1958 Allan Sandage made the first reasonably accurate measurement of the Hubble constant, the rate at which the universe expands, and his value came close to the range accepted ever since. Like Einstein, Sandage did not believe his own result, and he proposed new theories of how the universe began to explain the mismatch. The issue was largely settled once the models used to estimate the ages of stars improved. As of 2021, the oldest known stars come out at 14.27±0.80 billion years for the Methuselah star and 13.8±4 billion years for BD +17°3248, both in line with the Planck 2018 figure.

paragraphs.heading: A signal from the beginning
paragraphs.text: The 1965 announcement of the cosmic microwave background in effect ended the remaining doubt about the expanding universe. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Woodrow Wilson were using a very sensitive antenna to look for radio echoes when they picked up a low, steady microwave noise, spread evenly over the sky and present day and night. They became sure it came from beyond the Milky Way but could not explain it. Meanwhile a team less than 60 miles away, Robert Dicke, Jim Peebles and David Wilkinson, was hunting for faint noise left over from the Big Bang. The two teams realised the signal was radiation left from the Big Bang, and so strong evidence for the theory. Later the WMAP and Planck space probes, launched in 2001 and 2009, pinned down the Hubble constant and the age without relying on galaxy distances, which removed the largest source of error.
